chunks.text: Human Spaceflight Hazards 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight Astronauts encounter five hazards as they journey through space. Recognizing these hazards allows NASA to seek ways that overcome the challenges of sending humans to the space station, the Moon, Mars, and beyond. About the Five Hazards A human journey to Mars, at first glance, offers an inexhaustible amount of complexities. To bring such a mission to the Red Planet from fiction to fact, NASA’s Human Research Program has pinpointed five hazards that astronauts will encounter on their journeys. These include space radiation , isolation and confinement , distance from Earth , gravity (and the lack of it), and closed or hostile environments. Scroll down to learn details involving each hazard. Pooling the challenges of human spaceflight into categories allows for an organized effort to overcome the obstacles that lay before such a mission. However, these hazards do not stand alone. They can feed off one another and exacerbate effects on the human body, which are being studied using ground-based analogs , laboratories, and the International Space Station . These locations all serve as test beds to evaluate human performance, as well as the effectiveness of strategies that could keep astronauts safe and healthy in space. Through meticulous research, NASA is gaining valuable insight into how the human body and mind might respond during extended forays into space. The resulting data, technology, and methods serve as a knowledge bank from which scientists can extrapolate to multi-year interplanetary missions. Want a deeper dive? Explore different risks to human health linked to the five hazards of spaceflight. Distance from Earth Instructions, new supplies, medical care, and more become increasingly challenging to receive from Earth as astronauts venture deeper into space. Gravity Fields Astronauts' entire bodies – muscles, bones, inner ear, and organs – must adjust to the new gravities encountered on the space station or their spacecraft, as well as on the Moon, Mars, and Earth once they return home. Hostile/Closed Environments Maintaining a safe ecosystem inside a spacecraft presents unique challenges, from ensuring optimal temperatures, pressures, and lighting, to reducing noise, monitoring microbial communities, and tracking immune responses. Watch Videos Space Radiation This hazard of a human mission to Mars is the most difficult to visualize because, well, space radiation is invisible to the human eye. Radiation is not only stealthy, but considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight. Watch Isolation and Confinement Behavioral responses occur among groups of people isolated and confined in a small space over a long period of time. Crews must be carefully chosen, trained, and supported to ensure they can work effectively as a team for months or years in space. Watch Distance From Earth Mars is, on average, 140 million miles from Earth. Rather than a three-day lunar trip, astronauts would be leaving our planet for roughly three years. Planning and self-sufficiency will be key to successful deep space missions. Watch Gravity Fields On Mars, astronauts would need to live and work in three-eighths of Earth’s gravitational pull for up to two years. Throughout this time, their bodies – muscles, bones, inner ear, and organs – will be adjusting to new gravitational loads. Watch Hostile/Closed Environments A spacecraft is not only a home, it’s also a machine. The ecosystem inside a vehicle plays a big role in everyday astronaut life. Important habitability factors include temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, the presence of microbes, and more. Watch

Human Spaceflight Hazards Risks of Human Spaceflight NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) seeks to understand specific risks associated with the hazards of human spaceflight. Learn more about these risks below. About Human Spaceflight Risks NASA’s Human Research Program has identified several specific risks to human health associated with five hazards of spaceflight. The effects of these risks vary depending on whether humans are traveling to low Earth orbit, the Moon, or Mars. Learn more about each identified risk. Risks Involving Human Physiology Risks Involving Behavioral Performance Risks Involving Space Radiation For more background, explore the five hazards of human spaceflight . Risks Involving Human Physiology Risk of Altered Immune System Responses The stresses of spaceflight can awaken inactive viruses inside the bodies of astronauts, leading to rashes and other symptoms. Ongoing work seeks to further understand changes in the immune system to better protect astronaut health. Read About Altered Immune System Response Risks Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function Astronauts can experience motion sickness, issues with hand-eye or gait coordination, and dizziness during gravitational changes, making it difficult to walk or operate a vehicle. Ongoing research seeks to help astronauts recover faster from these changes so they can perform tasks inside and outside spacecraft. Read About Altered Function Risks Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Weightlessness alters blood circulation and how the heart and blood vessels function, potentially increasing the risk of cardiovascular events. Research focuses on minimizing these unhealthy changes. Read About Cardiovascular Adaptation Risks Risk of Decompression Sickness Transitioning from a pressurized spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit can cause health and mission complications when dissolved nitrogen starts to bubble within body tissues. Research focuses on developing better prevention and faster treatment options. Read About Decompression Sickness Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions Skin and gut microbiomes can change in space, potentially increasing the risk of crew members getting sick. To help keep crews healthy, researchers are exploring these microbial ecosystems and how they evolve in space. To help keep crews healthy, researchers are exploring these microbial ecosystems and how they evolve in space. Read About Host-Microorganism Interaction Risks Risk of Hypoxia Astronauts on future deep space missions will take steps to avoid “the bends” during spacewalks, but following those steps also elevates the risk of mild hypoxia — a condition that occurs when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal. Read About Hypoxia Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition A healthy, balanced diet is an essential element of crew health and performance. Ongoing research focuses on designing enjoyable, long-lasting, and nutritious meals for deep space missions and understanding the consequences of inadequate nutrition. Read About Inadequate Food and Nutrition Risks Risk of Injury and Compromised Performance from Spacewalks Working in a spacesuit is challenging. In addition to cognitive fatigue and injury, crew members must also manage risks in the spacewalk environment, including decompression sickness, and low oxygen and high carbon dioxide levels. Research focuses on characterizing human performance in spacesuits and balancing pressure and oxygen levels. Read About Spacewalk Risks Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness All astronauts perform exercise during their mission to counteract losses in bone density, muscle strength, and heart and blood vessel performance. Researchers are studying what types of exercise will best protect their health and their ability to perform spacewalks. Read About Reduced Fitness Risks Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) The structure of the eyes and brain can change with spaceflight. Research focuses on understanding the long-term health consequences of these changes and preventing them from occurring. Read About SANS Risks Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes Without gravity, bones break down and become more brittle, boosting the chances of painful breaks. Ongoing research seeks to better understand and quantify these losses, and help preserve bone strength through diet, exercise, and medication. Read About Spaceflight-Induced Bone Change Risks Risks Involving Behavioral Performance and Human Factors Risk of Behavioral Changes

Ongoing research seeks to better understand and quantify these losses, and help preserve bone strength through diet, exercise, and medication. Read About Spaceflight-Induced Bone Change Risks Risks Involving Behavioral Performance and Human Factors Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth, and other intense space stressors may all take a toll on the mental health of the crew. Ongoing research seeks to better understand and quantify these psychological risks. Read About Behavioral and Psychiatric Risks Risk of Inadequate Teamwork Selecting a crew that works well together is essential for mission success and safety. Researchers are studying how to help teams in prolonged isolation and confinement function efficiently and quickly recover after setbacks occur. They’re also mapping the myriad risks from miscommunications and related team tensions. Read About Inadequate Teamwork Risks Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules Space crews experience multiple hazards simultaneously. Stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands, and irregularities in their internal biological clocks. Understanding how to reduce the effects of these stressors on crew health and safety is an ongoing area of research. Read About Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedule Risks Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support Future crews on deep space missions must be able to live and work in an environment where they may face unexpected problems with software, vehicles, or other systems. Research focuses on understanding when crews need information, the types and timing of required training, or other support options. Read About Inadequate Support Risks Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads During landing activities, crews risk getting injured. Understanding the likelihood of such injuries and how to better prevent them are areas of ongoing research. Monitoring radiation for astronaut health Canadian Space Agency ( CSA ) astronaut David Saint-Jacques using bubble detectors, a predecessor to Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), on the International Space Station ( ISS ). (Credits: CSA / NASA ) 2026-02-26 Radiation is one of the key challenges faced by astronauts living and working beyond the protective shield of Earth’s atmosphere. As Canada and its international partners advance plans for missions to the Moon, and eventually Mars, the CSA continues to invest in technology to better understand exposure levels. The CSA has awarded a contract of $5.5 million to Bubble Technology Industries for the continued development of the CANS , a compact and autonomous instrument designed to measure neutron radiation exposure in space. Neutron radiation, which contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS , is especially harmful because it can cause serious biological damage and require specialized protective measures. For over 25 years, the ISS has been a test bed for new technology. Canada has significant expertise in radiation detection experiments on the ISS , including MOSFET , EVARM and Radi-N and Radi-N2 . CANS improves upon previous radiation detection methods with the unique combined capabilities of working continuously and autonomously. Data collected could help develop better measures to reduce risks for astronauts’ health and also has potential applications on Earth, including cancer therapy, radiation protection for aircrews, nuclear threat detection and public safety, among others.

Why do we conduct science experiments in space? Science is our quest for more knowledge about the world and ourselves. For thousands of years, humanity has pushed boundaries in its search to learn more about our place in the universe. Canadian science on the International Space Station Canada's participation in the International Space Station ( ISS ) allows our scientists to access the unique space environment and conduct cutting-edge experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory to: prepare for deep-space destinations use the knowledge obtained to improve our quality of life on Earth Ok Did you know that many science experiments are being conducted on the ISS at any given time? Why do we do science in space? (Credit: Canadian Space Agency) ( Transcript ) Preparing for deep-space destinations As space agencies from all over the world are looking to propel humanity further into the solar system, Canada's space science community continues to conduct research aboard the ISS . We want to better understand the risks associated with human space flight—and help find countermeasures and treatments—to identify, characterize, and mitigate the effects on astronauts' health in order to make space travel safer. Missions to the Moon and Mars mean longer trips and more risks for astronauts, including: more time in weightlessness more exposure to radiation longer periods of isolation, very far from home increased delays in communication with Earth less ability to rely on Earth for food, materials, and emergency medical assistance Using the knowledge obtained to improve our quality of life on Earth Studying the way our body changes in space help us understand the impacts of reduced levels of physical activity and issues that affect older adult populations on Earth. Living in weightless conditions changes the human body in many ways. The effects observed in astronauts are similar to accelerated aging and health problems caused by a sedentary lifestyle . Studying the human body in space for six months gives us data that would take years to gather on Earth. New information gained in space contributes to improved quality of life on Earth . Canadian scientists use space to study

Living in weightless conditions changes the human body in many ways. The effects observed in astronauts are similar to accelerated aging and health problems caused by a sedentary lifestyle . Studying the human body in space for six months gives us data that would take years to gather on Earth. New information gained in space contributes to improved quality of life on Earth . Canadian scientists use space to study our bones, heart, blood vessels and brain. Their experiments have produced findings that can help people suffering from balance problems , such as seniors; osteoporosis ; cardiovascular disorders; and Type-2 diabetes . Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Lumbar Spine Paraspinal Muscle and Intervertebral Disc Height Changes in Astronauts After Long-Duration Spaceflight on the International Space Station. Authors/institution: Chang DG et al.. Year: 2016. Evidence and environment: Human flight, longitudinal MRI; six ISS crewmembers; Earth recovery. Source sections reviewed: Materials and Methods; Results; Discussion. Findings and applicability limits: Lower-back discomfort, lumbar spine, paraspinal muscles, multifidus, disc height. MRI demonstrated reduced functional paraspinal muscle cross-sectional area after long-duration flight, with incomplete recovery at follow-up. The study did not demonstrate generalized intervertebral disc-height expansion. These are small-cohort imaging observations, not evidence identifying the cause of a reported episode of back pain. Atrophy does not establish an acute muscle injury, herniation, or the cause of swelling. Results concern ISS exposure and terrestrial recovery, not observations during lunar or Martian residence.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Shoulder Injury Overview & Treatment Guidance. Authors/institution: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer. Year: 2025. Evidence and environment: Official technical synthesis; Earth-based NBL EVA training and surveillance. Source sections reviewed: History of Shoulder Injuries in Astronauts; Design of the EMU Planar HUT. Findings and applicability limits: Shoulder pain, reduced movement, limited range of motion, overhead tasks, spacesuit fit. The brief discusses restrictions on normal shoulder mechanics associated with the extravehicular mobility unit hard upper torso, repetitive motion, tools, and inverted training positions. Training surveillance is distinct from observing an injury during flight. This material does not identify the cause of a swollen or painful shoulder after exercise in microgravity. General muscle deconditioning cannot by itself explain acute focal swelling or functional limitation. Only the historical and suit-mechanics material is summarized here; clinical treatment tables and medication guidance are excluded.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: High intensity training during spaceflight: results from the NASA Sprint Study. Authors/institution: English KL et al.. Year: 2020. Evidence and environment: Human ISS exercise comparison; 26 astronauts; nine Sprint and 17 controls. Source sections reviewed: Methods: research design and subjects; Results; Tables 1–5. Findings and applicability limits: Muscle strength, endurance, trunk and lower-limb function, exercise, aerobic deconditioning. Astronauts self-selected into exercise groups. Physiological outcomes were broadly comparable between the programs, while some postflight decrements remained. Exercise participation therefore does not establish complete preservation of every measured outcome. Strength, endurance, bone density and task performance are different measurements. Changing standard care and nonrandom allocation limit causal interpretation. This study does not diagnose exercise-associated pain or swelling, prescribe a personal training program, or establish readiness for an extravehicular activity.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Incomplete recovery of bone strength and trabecular microarchitecture at the distal tibia 1 year after return from long duration spaceflight. Authors/institution: Gabel L et al.. Year: 2022. Evidence and environment: Human longitudinal cohort; 17 astronauts; preflight and Earth recovery at six/twelve months. Source sections reviewed: Results; Tables 1–2; Methods. Findings and applicability limits: Bone loss, distal tibia, radius, trabecular microarchitecture, estimated bone strength, readaptation. Imaging showed incomplete recovery of some tibial outcomes one year after long-duration flight. Skeletal sites and participants differed; findings at the radius cannot be substituted for those at the tibia. Failure load is an imaging-based strength estimate, not a count of actual fractures. These population findings cannot calculate an individual fracture probability from heart rate, steps, pain or a wearable. The study does not establish the cause of lower-limb pain or authorize activity clearance.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Keeping Pace with Wearables: A Living Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews Evaluating the Accuracy of Consumer Wearable Technologies in Health Measurement. Authors/institution: Doherty C et al.. Year: 2024. Evidence and environment: Terrestrial consumer-device validation umbrella review; 24 systematic reviews. Source sections reviewed: Methods; Sections 3.4–3.9; Discussion and limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Wearable accuracy, heart rate, SpO2, steps, sleep duration and energy expenditure. Accuracy depends on the specific device, outcome, firmware, population, activity and reference instrument. Heterogeneity prevented an individual-study meta-analysis. A pooled estimate from other watches is not an error specification for Amazfit Active 2. Brand similarity does not validate a model, and terrestrial validation does not establish validity in microgravity or partial gravity. Total sleep duration, sleep efficiency, stages and perceived quality are distinct outcomes. A step count is not a validated cross-environment measure of exercise loading.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: The performance of 11 fingertip pulse oximeters during hypoxemia in healthy human participants with varied, quantified skin pigment. Authors/institution: Leeb G et al.. Year: 2024. Evidence and environment: Controlled terrestrial desaturation; 34 healthy participants; eleven fingertip devices. Source sections reviewed: Methods; Findings; Discussion and limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Pulse oximetry, SpO2, arterial oxygen saturation SaO2, skin pigmentation and measurement bias. Performance varied across tested fingertip oximeters, including differences associated with skin pigmentation. The reference comparison used arterial measurements. These results do not validate a wrist sensor, the Active 2, or use during spaceflight. A single watch estimate cannot establish a diagnosis or determine an oxygen prescription. Device type, reference method and measurement conditions must remain attached to accuracy statements. This experiment does not quantify every possible motion or perfusion artifact, and its findings must not be turned into a universal correction for watch readings.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Smart Devices and Wearable Technologies to Detect and Monitor Mental Health Conditions and Stress: A Systematic Review. Authors/institution: Hickey BA et al.. Year: 2021. Evidence and environment: Systematic review of terrestrial smart-device mental-health/stress studies. Source sections reviewed: Abstract; stress subsection; Discussion and limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Wearable stress, physiological arousal, heart rate, heart-rate variability HRV, electrodermal activity and self-report. Studies used different signals and assessment methods; HRV was prominent in stress research. Average heart rate and HRV are not interchangeable. Research on these signals does not validate an arbitrary proprietary stress score. This review does not provide a score-to-diagnosis conversion for Amazfit Active 2 or establish anxiety severity in an astronaut. A device stress indicator, a daily mood questionnaire and a clinical assessment are separate kinds of information. Heterogeneous terrestrial studies cannot establish diagnostic accuracy during isolation or microgravity.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Circadian misalignment affects sleep and medication use before and during spaceflight. Authors/institution: Flynn-Evans EE et al.. Year: 2016. Evidence and environment: Observational human ISS study; 21 participants; actigraphy/light data and modeled circadian phase. Source sections reviewed: Results; circadian alignment classification; limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Sleep timing, circadian misalignment, sleep duration and fatigue. Modeled misalignment was associated with shorter sleep episodes. Observational associations do not establish the cause of one person’s fatigue. Sleep duration alone does not reveal circadian phase, sleep architecture, fragmentation or subjective sleep quality. The analysis used research data beyond a single total-sleep-duration value. Some ISS sleep data overlap with the Barger observational work, so these documents are not independent replication. This summary does not provide hypnotic recommendations, diagnose insomnia, or establish individual performance readiness.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Human Biomechanical and Cardiopulmonary Responses to Partial Gravity – A Systematic Review. Authors/institution: Richter C et al.. Year: 2017. Evidence and environment: Systematic review; 43 studies; Apollo evidence and terrestrial analogs; no long-term studies. Source sections reviewed: Eligibility; simulation-model classification; Results; limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Lunar gravity, Martian gravity, partial gravity, hypogravity, locomotion and mechanical loading. Acute biomechanical and cardiopulmonary responses differ across gravity conditions and simulation methods. Body-weight support, parabolic flight and planetary surface operations are not equivalent exposures. None of the included studies examined long-term effects. Predictions about chronic adaptation must remain identified as predictions. Equal step counts cannot be assumed to represent equal ground reaction forces, energy expenditure or exercise loads across Earth, Moon and Mars. This evidence cannot quantify an individual’s six-month muscle loss on Mars or supply a validated planetary exercise prescription.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions. Authors/institution: Stahn AC et al.. Year: 2017. Evidence and environment: Repeated measurements in eleven ISS astronauts; terrestrial comparison. Source sections reviewed: Methods: temperature sensor; resting/exercise Results; limitations. Findings and applicability limits: Temperature, core body temperature, heat-flux sensor, thermoregulation and exercise. Research using a forehead heat-flux approach observed different resting and exercise temperature responses during long-duration flight compared with terrestrial measurements. Measurement site, method, timing and activity state matter. A manually entered spot temperature or skin temperature is not automatically comparable to the study’s core-temperature estimate. The small cohort and particular sensor limit generalization. Associations with inflammatory markers do not prove a causal mechanism. These observations cannot diagnose infection or fever from an isolated user entry or define a personal safe exercise limit.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: The Effects of Long Duration Spaceflight on Sensorimotor Control and Cognition. Authors/institution: Tays GD et al.. Year: 2021. Evidence and environment: Human longitudinal study; fifteen astronauts; six-month ISS missions and Earth recovery. Source sections reviewed: Functional Mobility/SOT methods; Results; recovery analyses. Findings and applicability limits: Balance, mobility, bimanual coordination, sensory reweighting and functional limitation. Sensorimotor task performance changed around long-duration flight, while selected cognitive measures were maintained. Different tests measure different functions; recovery should not be reduced to a universal date for every astronaut or outcome. Small samples, task selection and practice effects limit inference. Reported movement difficulty cannot be attributed to muscle strength alone, and a pain rating is not a substitute for task testing. This study does not diagnose vestibular disease or clear a person for exercise, walking, landing tasks or EVA.

Reviewed evidence summary, not the complete publication. Source: Space radiation measurements during the Artemis I lunar mission. Authors/institution: George SP et al.. Year: 2024. Evidence and environment: Physical dosimetry; uncrewed Artemis I Orion; detectors and instrumented torso phantoms. Source sections reviewed: Detector configuration; shielding comparisons; Methods and unit definitions. Findings and applicability limits: Radiation exposure, absorbed dose, dose equivalent, shielding, cabin location and dosimetry. Measurements depended on location, shielding and mission conditions. This was an uncrewed mission, not a study measuring clinical symptoms in astronauts. Selecting a Moon or Mars environment in software does not supply dosimeter measurements or a trajectory-specific exposure model. Heart rate, SpO2, sleep and reported symptoms cannot calculate a personal radiation dose from this study. Physical exposure measurements must remain separate from biological risk estimates and individual diagnoses. Findings should not be transferred unchanged to different spacecraft, shielding, trajectories or solar conditions.
